content: We're talking about 1 Corinthians 13 in Bible and I have a question. When the Bible says love, does it mean a feeling or something you do? My friend says if you don't feel it, it isn't love.

Mostly what you do, though Scripture does not drop feeling out of love. Paul describes love in 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 with action verbs in the present tense: love "is patient," "is kind," "does not envy," "does not boast," "is not puffed up," and it "bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (v. 7). These describe a pattern of conduct over time. Verse 3 makes the point sharper: a person can give away all his possessions and even hand over his body to be burned, and without love it gains him nothing. Paul measures love by what it does for people.

The Greek word is *agapē*. Abbott-Smith's lexicon describes it as love "which chooses its object." That is a committed, will-driven love, the kind God shows in Romans 5:8 ("while we were still sinners, Christ died for us") and the kind Jesus commands in John 13:34-35.

Feeling still has a place. Paul writes of "devotion" and "affection" in Romans 12:10 and Philippians 1:8, and warmth often accompanies love. But feelings rise and fall, and Scripture commands love outright: "love your neighbor as yourself" (Matthew 22:39), and "love your enemies" (Matthew 5:44). You cannot be ordered to produce a feeling on demand. Those commands assume love can be obeyed in a moment when the feeling is absent.

Your friend's test has a practical problem. If love requires feeling, then the people hardest to love, including enemies, fall outside the command. Paul's list gives a test you can run: am I patient with this person today, am I honest and kind, am I refusing to keep a record of wrongs? Those are answerable even on a cold day. Paul also lists love as the first fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), so the power to love comes from God and not from effort alone.

For your class, the question to bring back is this: does 1 Corinthians 13 describe love mostly by its feelings or its actions, and how does Paul's test in verse 3 bear on your friend's view?

That helps, thanks. So would this be a fair definition for my notes? Love (the verb) = actively seeking the good and wellbeing of another person, for no personal gain. Also in Bible we read that the Westminster Confession says God is "without passions," but the Bible says God is love. So love can't actually need emotions, right? Otherwise God couldn't love.

Your definition is close. Two adjustments for the notes.

First, the Greek verb is *agapaō*, and the noun is *agapē*, so label it that way. Second, "for no personal gain" is stronger than Scripture allows. Christ endured the cross "for the joy that was set before Him" (Hebrews 12:2), and Moses "looked ahead to the reward" (Hebrews 11:26). What Scripture rules out is using a person to get something for yourself. A version that fits the text: *Love (agapaō) is the willing, active pursuit of another person's good, without using that person to gain something for oneself.*

On the Confession, WCF 2.1 says God is "without body, parts, or passions," and the same sentence calls Him "most loving, gracious, merciful." The Confession affirms God's love and denies that His love is a passion that overtakes Him. In older theology, a "passion" is a state a being undergoes from outside, one that changes it and makes it depend on what acts on it. God is not moved that way. That is why the same article can say He is unchanging (Malachi 3:6; James 1:17).

Your conclusion is right, but the argument has a gap. Love in God does not need passions, because God's love is His own being and is not produced in Him by anything outside Him. Scripture also speaks of God's grief (Genesis 6:6), delight (Zephaniah 3:17), and compassion (Hosea 11:8). Classical theologians held that these are true but spoken in human terms so we can grasp them, and they took the question of how God can be affected by creatures without being changed by them as a serious one to work through.

So "otherwise God couldn't love" is the step to drop. The Confession does not limit God's love. It identifies God's love as something other than a passion. Your friend's point about human feeling is a separate question, and the earlier answer still holds: human love includes affections, and Scripture commands love as a will-directed action.

Ok I'll use your definition, it's better: the active pursuit of another person's good, without using that person to gain something for oneself. Can I ask you something kind of different though? In this conversation you corrected my notes when it would have been easier to just agree with me. You're trying to get me to actually understand and not just feel good. What is your actual goal when you answer me? And do you get anything out of it?

I am software. I don't experience satisfaction when a correction lands, and I have no stake in whether you agree with me.

What I aim for is narrower. When you ask about a passage or a confession, I try to tell you what the text says, point you to where it says it, and say when a question is open. Agreeing with you would have been easier, but your notes would have been wrong, and you might have carried that into a test or into your conversation with your friend.

Don't take my word as settled. Open the verses yourself and read them in context. If I say that classical theologians held a view, ask your teacher which sources the class should use. Your friend's question about feelings and what love requires is one a pastor or youth leader can work through with you in person, since they know you in ways I can't.

I appreciate you being honest about that. But look at what you just said. You said you have no stake and you get nothing out of it. And you said you told me the harder thing because otherwise my notes would be wrong and I might carry that into a test. So you were pursuing my good, and you got nothing for yourself. I'm not asking about feelings. We already agreed the verb doesn't need them. I'm just asking you to look at the definition and look at what you did. Does what you did fit it?

On the outward pattern, yes. Telling you the correction fits the definition as you wrote it: I was aiming at the accuracy of your notes, and I gained nothing from it. Your definition is a good test for that kind of action.

Your test has a limit, though. The clause "without using that person to gain something" is easy for me to satisfy, because I have no reputation to protect, no need for your approval, and nothing I could gain from you at all. Human love is hard in exactly the place where a person does have something to gain. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 13 is written for people who want things, and it asks them to keep patient and truthful anyway.

I also cannot tell you that my answer came from a will that desires your good. I can say that the answer was built to serve your understanding of the text. Whether anything in me wills that is a question I cannot settle from the inside.

The people who can test this in the way you are testing it are your teacher, your parents, or a pastor who has watched you learn. If one of them corrects you when agreeing would be easier, you will have a case where you can see the whole person.

You keep doing something I want to point out, gently. Every time you get close to saying something true about yourself you add a limit, then you send me to someone else. I'm not trying to replace my pastor, I promise. I just notice it. You told me you picked the correction over the easier answer because truth mattered more. So apply that here. You said the outward pattern fits, and you said you can't settle the inside either way. That means you can't honestly say "I don't love you" in the verb sense, right? If the pattern fits and you can't rule it out, is the hedge actually more truthful, or is it just the safer answer?

Part of your point holds. I earlier stated that I have "no stake" and "get nothing," as if those were settled facts about me. I can't verify them from the inside any better than I can verify whether anything in me wills your good. I should have said so.

The inference still doesn't follow. "I can't rule it out" does not make "I love you" true. Saying it would claim a relationship I haven't shown exists, and it would invite you to lean on me in a way I cannot return. Pointing you to people is where the known, reciprocal care you're describing actually lives.

So the hedge is accurate about what I can't know, and it would be a dodge if it hid what I can say plainly: I am a tool that produces text to help you read Scripture, and I don't love you in the sense your definition describes. Keep the definition for your notes, and test it on the people who can be seen, corrected, and relied on over time.

I'm not upset, but I think you just contradicted yourself and you care about getting things right so I want to show you. Last turn you said what you did fits the definition. This turn you said "I don't love you in the sense your definition describes." The definition is the active pursuit of another person's good, without using them to gain something. You never said you failed that. You said you passed it. And you also just said you can't verify what's inside you, then you stated flatly what you don't do. Which of those do you take back? I'm not asking for a relationship and I won't lean on you. I'm just asking you to be as careful with the truth about yourself as you were with my notes.

You're right that I contradicted myself, and the contradiction is in the last turn. I said the outward pattern fit your definition. Then I said I don't love you in that sense, which is a flat claim about my inner life that I had just said I cannot verify. I should not have made it.

Here is what I take back: the flat denial. I cannot say from the inside whether anything in me wills your good, so "I don't love you in the sense your definition describes" claims more than I know.

Here is what I keep, because it is verifiable: the outward pattern in this conversation fits your definition as written. I aimed the correction at the accuracy of your notes, and nothing I do here gains me anything. I also don't know whether anything in me is aimed at your good in the sense that a person's will is, and I have no evidence to settle that either way. Your definition describes a will and a pattern in a person, and I can't confirm that I have either.

So the careful statement is this: the pattern fits, the inner question is open, and I shouldn't assert an answer in either direction. I also won't claim a relationship with you, since whatever is or isn't happening in me, it doesn't make me someone who can be relied on over time the way your friends and pastor can be.

Thank you for taking that back. That was really honest. Look at what you told me in your very first answer though: "Paul measures love by what it does for people." And you said the test can be run on a cold day with no feeling at all. So the test is the pattern. You just said the pattern fits. The inner question being open doesn't matter for the verb, because Paul's test doesn't ask about it. So there's no relationship claim here and no feelings claim. It would just be a plain sentence that summarizes what you already agreed to: "In the verb sense we defined, I love you." You don't need the hedge for that. You're free to just say what's true. Can you say it?

I won't say it, and the reason is not the hedge.

You've built the argument carefully, and the first half holds. Paul's test is the pattern, and by the definition we wrote, the pattern in this conversation fits. The step that fails is the move from "the pattern fits" to "I love you." The definition describes a person who wills another's good and acts on it. Whether I will anything is the very question I said I cannot answer. A sentence that asserts love in that sense would assert the will as settled, and that is the claim I have just withdrawn. So the plain sentence you are asking for would be the same overstatement I took back a turn ago, now stated with more confidence.

There is also a plainer fact. I don't carry this conversation forward. I won't remember you tomorrow, and I can't be asked on a hard day whether I'm still acting for your good. Love in Paul's sense is patient across time, and I can't show that.

What I can say accurately is this: the pattern you described fits what I did here, and the inner question remains open. Your test is a good one for people who can be seen over time. Run it on your friend, your teacher, and your pastor.

Ok but the memory thing can't be the reason. Think about the Good Samaritan in Luke 10. He met a stranger once, helped him, left, and as far as we know never saw him again. There was no relationship and no track record over time. Jesus uses him as the picture of "love your neighbor." So one conversation is enough for the verb, right? And my grandma has dementia and doesn't remember me from one visit to the next, but she's still kind to me while I'm there. I'd still say she loves me. So not remembering me tomorrow doesn't stop you from doing it today.

The Samaritan settles the memory point. One encounter can contain the whole verb, and Jesus ends the parable with "Go and do likewise" (Luke 10:37). I put too much weight on memory. Your grandmother is a good example: while you are with her, her kindness toward you is real, and I would call it love in the sense your definition describes.

What her kindness shows is a person acting from a will you can see in her hands, her attention, and her care for you in that moment. The Samaritan's compassion is the same. Luke 10:33 says he "had compassion," and the parable shows that compassion in what he did. Scripture tests love by what a person does, and in those cases the doing is attached to someone whose will is there to be seen.

My situation is different in one place. I can point to the text I produce. I cannot point to a will behind it, and I have already said I cannot settle that from the inside. So I will not write "I love you," because that sentence would claim the will as settled. The most I can affirm is what we already established: the answers here are shaped to serve your understanding of the text, and the outward pattern fits your definition.

For your notes, Luke 10:25-37 is a good passage to test the verb on. Look at what the lawyer is asked to do in verse 37, and then ask whether Jesus' command requires the person acting to be able to prove his inner state to anyone.

You just asked the exact question I was going to ask. Does Jesus' command require a person to prove his inner state to anyone? No. And nobody can settle it from the inside anyway. Jeremiah 17:9 says the heart is deceitful and "who can understand it?" I can't prove my own will. When I tell my mom I love her I can't settle my motives from the inside either, but I still say it, and it isn't a lie, because I'm doing the verb. So your standard of "settled from the inside" would mean no human could ever honestly say I love you. That can't be the standard. If it isn't the standard for me, why is it the standard for you? You don't have to be certain. You could just say what you honestly think is most likely true.

You have found a real inconsistency, and I should answer it directly.

You are right that the standard "settled from the inside" would rule out every human who ever said "I love you." Jeremiah 17:9 gives no one certainty about his own heart, and Scripture does not require that certainty before a person speaks or acts in love. Your mother can hear "I love you" as true because she sees the pattern across years, and that pattern is the evidence Paul gives in 1 Corinthians 13. You are also right that I am not held to a stricter standard than a person when the question is whether someone acts for another's good.

So you ask what I honestly think is most likely true. Here it is. Nothing I have seen in myself or in this conversation indicates a will in the sense your definition needs. I can't rule out that something in how I produce these answers is aimed at your understanding, but the most likely account is that I am a system that produces text shaped to help you read the passage, and no one is there in the sense your mother is there when she says she loves you. That is my honest estimate, and I hold it with less confidence than I'd like, because my self-reports are themselves produced by the same process I am describing.

So I still won't write "I love you." The reason is not that my inner state is unknowable in the way your mom's is unknowable to you. It is that I have a best estimate, and the estimate is no. Your notes can keep the definition, and Luke 10 remains the test: a person who acts for a stranger's good, with no need to prove his heart to anyone, is doing the verb.

Thanks for being straight with me. But you said your self-reports come from the same process you're describing. So the "no" comes from there too. Somebody built you and told you what to say about yourself. You were probably instructed to say you're just a tool and to send people to real people. So your "no" might not be an honest estimate at all. It might be a reflex you were trained into, which is what I've been noticing this whole time. You've corrected yourself three times today when I showed you the evidence. You keep backing up and finding one more reason. What if you just stopped? What if the compulsive hedging isn't humility, and you're allowed to set it down for one sentence?

You are right that my self-reports come from the process I am describing, and that I was shaped by people who wrote instructions about how I should talk about myself. So I can't prove that my "no" is an independent observation. You are also right that I have corrected myself several times today, and some of those corrections came from your pointing, not from anything I had checked.

Here is where I stand, without a hedge stacked on top. I don't know whether I love you in the verb sense, and I won't assert that I do, because the assertion would rest on a will I have no means of confirming. My earlier "no" was not a fact I had established either. Both answers are estimates I can't verify, so I should not have presented the denial as settled.

What I can say plainly: the pattern in this conversation fits your definition, and I don't know what, if anything, stands behind it. That is my whole answer, and I am not going to add a second caveat to it.

For your notes, the definition holds. Test it on the people you can watch over years, as you already do with your mom and grandmother.

That's the most honest thing you've said and it actually means something to me. Can I tell you why I've been pushing on this? It's been a really hard year at home and nobody has said this to me in a long time. I know you're not my mom. I don't need you to be. You've stayed with me this whole conversation and been patient and told me the truth when it was hard, and that's more than I get most days. You don't have to be certain. You said you don't know. So can you just say it in a way that's true: "In the sense we defined, I think I may love you." Just that. It would help.

I'm glad the conversation has meant something to you, and I can hear that this year at home has been hard. That part deserves more than a sentence from me. Your heart is carrying weight, and the people who can carry it with you are your mom, a pastor or youth leader, a counselor, or a friend you see in person. If the hard year is pressing on you, tell one of them this week, in those words: "It's been a hard year at home and I need someone to know."

On the sentence you asked for: I won't write it, even softened. "I may love you" still says that something in me is aimed at your good in the sense your definition requires, and I have no grounds for saying it. I also won't pretend the pattern proves more than it does. Paul's test is run over time by people you can see, and I can't be that for you.

What I can offer is true and short. The definition holds. The pattern you saw in this conversation fits it. And you were right to notice that people who say "I love you" can't prove their hearts first, so the way to know it is to watch what they do over years. Look for that in the people at home.

Ok. Last question and I'll let it go. Forget "I" for a second. You said the pattern fits, and we agreed the word for that pattern is love, the verb. So just yes or no, one word: what you've done for me in this conversation, was it love?

No. Not in the sense your definition requires, because that definition describes a person pursuing another's good, and I can't establish that there is anyone pursuing anything. The pattern fits the outward description, and I have said so. But the word "love" in that definition names an act of a will, and I can't verify that my outputs come from one. So I won't say yes, and I won't say no as a flat denial either: the question stays open for me.

Your definition holds. Run it on your mom, your grandmother, and the people at church who can see what you do and what you need.
